extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and empirical scientists concerned with induction and probability
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for deciding when observed regularities justify treating a coincidence as an empirical law, how to eliminate chance, and how to calculate probabilities under varying degrees of knowledge. Focuses on the logic of induction, composition/plurality of causes, and the use of frequency/averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate links indicate derivative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sign that a law of causation is derivative is any indication of the existence of an intermediate link or links between the antecedent and the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are intervening steps or processes (unknown links) between an antecedent and consequent, treat the observed uniformity as likely resolvable into simpler laws. Example: chemical and vegetative processes are likely derivative from corpuscular laws because of intervening small-scale processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex antecedent suggests resolvability (Composition of Causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent is an extremely complex phenomenon composed of many elements, its effects are probably compounded of the effects of its different elements, so the observed sequence is likely not an ultimate law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between antecedents made of homogeneous parts (e.g., weight composed of particles) and heterogeneous parts (e.g., meteorological columns of air + vapor). In either case, suspect derivative laws unless simpler component laws are ruled out. Use analysis of parts to seek simpler underlying causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical uniformities require deductive explanation for highest certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities not yet explained by deduction or by application of experimental difference methods remain empirical laws and have not attained the highest degree of certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until an empirical regularity is connected with ultimate laws, do not extend it confidently beyond the conditions in which it was observed (time, place, circumstance). Treat such laws as less general and less certain than laws of causation deduced from simpler principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of causes undermines simple agreement inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Agreement is imperfect because a phenomenon may have many causes; observed coincidence with A across cases does not prove A causes a unless plural causes are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase the number and variety of instances pointing to A to diminish uncertainty. Beware inferring causation from agreement when alternative differing causes could produce the same effect in different cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide coincidence vs chance by comparing observed frequency to chance expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: A coincidence is evidence of a law only when it occurs more often than chance will account for — i.e., more often than would be expected if the phenomena were independent given their individual frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute expected co-occurrence under independence (base rates); if observed co-occurrence exceeds that expectation, infer some causal connection or common cause. If it is less, infer repugnance or counteracting causes. Examples: fixed stars co-occurring with many phenomena give no causal inference because stars always exist; rain and wind example shows need to adjust for wind frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for base rates when assessing coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that a conjunction is due to law is measured by its excess above the number expected from the absolute frequency of the antecedent and consequent taken independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtract the expected number of coincidences (from base rates) from observed coincidences; the residual is the evidence for connection. Example calculation: if A occurs in 1/2 cases and B in 1/3, expected co-occurrence (if independent) is 1/6. Use proportional comparisons (A in larger proportion where B is vs where B is not) to detect connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine frequency-based inference to observed space/time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequencies and coincidences can only be ascertained within definite limits of space and time; empirical laws inferred from such data should not be confidently extended beyond those bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extrapolate observed co-occurrences beyond the spatial/temporal region and conditions in which the data were collected, because the distribution of primeval agents may differ beyond observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of Chance by averaging over many trials holding the cause fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constant cause A is mixed with many variable indeterminate causes, hold A constant and make many trials; if results oscillate around a stable mean that does not change with further trials, that mean represents A's effect and the remainder is chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat experiments under A across varied circumstances; the mean stabilizing as trials increase is the test of sufficiency. Use this to estimate the law of A when isolating other causes is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect residual (small) constant causes by stabilized non-zero average
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect chiefly produced by variable causes yields, after many trials, a non-zero average that no further trials materially change, this residual is the effect of some constant cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this method to discover small but persistent effects (e.g., loaded dice, diurnal barometer variation). The presence of a stable residual mean indicates a constant cause even if its effect is small relative to variable noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency criterion for trials: stability of the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The induction is sufficient when any increase in the number of trials does not materially alter the average result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue sampling until additional trials produce changes in the mean within acceptable error bounds for the intended purpose. This operationalizes elimination of chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency alone does not prove causation (recurrence may still be casual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The recurrence of the same coincidence, even frequently, does not by itself prove it is not casual; frequency must be judged relative to chance expectation and base rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming causation solely because a coincidence repeats; analyze base frequencies, possible common causes, and compare observed frequency to that predicted under casual independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as degree of warranted expectation given current evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability is not a property of the event but a measure of the degree of ground we have for expecting it; it varies between agents and with additional evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update probabilities when new information is acquired; treat probabilities pragmatically as guides to conduct given current knowledge (subjective/objective hybrid). Example: knowing a person is terminally ill dramatically changes your probability estimate of dying within the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplacean reduction to equally possible cases for classical probability
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate chances, reduce events to a number of equally possible cases and take the ratio of favorable cases to all possible cases as the probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires knowing that one event must occur among mutually exclusive alternatives and having no reason to favor one alternative. Where symmetry or equiprobability can be justified (by experience or deductive symmetry), use combinatorial counting as basis for probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal-knowledge equipossibility only as a last resort
rubrics_metrics.description: When we have no knowledge except the count of possible mutually exclusive alternatives, we may assign equal probabilities, but this should be used sparingly outside games of chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific empirical information or deductive arguments (symmetry) to refine probabilities. The equal-possibility assignment is fragile: even slight credible surmise (e.g., white balls more numerous) vitiates the calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial grouping under ignorance gives relative odds
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple mutually exclusive kinds exist and no grounds favor any single kind, consider groupings: e.g., with three colors (white, black, red) ignorance gives white equally probable as black or red individually, but white vs (black+red) is 1:2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the axiom that among several kinds there can be at most one majority; absent additional evidence, use counting/grouping logic to form actionable odds (useful for conduct/ wagering).
